claim: Heat shock induces a conserved transcriptional program regulated by heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) in eukaryotic cells.
source: Heat shock induces a conserved transcriptional program regulated by heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Activation of the heat shock response is triggered by heat-induced misfolding of newly synthesized polypeptides.
source: Activation of this heat shock response is triggered by heat-induced misfolding of newly synthesized polypeptides, and so has been thought to depend on ongoing protein synthesis.
evidence: This represents the prevailing model in the field prior to this study.

claim: Hsf1 can be robustly activated when protein synthesis is inhibited, so long as cells undergo cytosolic acidification.
source: Here, using the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we report the discovery that Hsf1 can be robustly activated when protein synthesis is inhibited, so long as cells undergo cytosolic acidification.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Heat shock causes transient intracellular acidification in eukaryotes.
source: Heat shock has long been known to cause transient intracellular acidification which, for reasons which have remained unclear, is associated with increased stress resistance in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Weitzel et al., 1987; Bright and Ellis, 1992; Munder et al., 2016; Kroschwald et al., 2015) and confirmed by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Acidification is required for heat shock response induction in translationally inhibited cells.
source: We demonstrate that acidification is required for heat shock response induction in translationally inhibited cells, and specifically affects Hsf1 activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 2D, 2E, and 3.

claim: Physiological heat-triggered acidification increases population fitness.
source: Physiological heat-triggered acidification also increases population fitness and promotes cell cycle reentry following heat shock.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6B showing growth rate differences as a function of pH during stress.

claim: Physiological heat-triggered acidification promotes cell cycle reentry following heat shock.
source: Physiological heat-triggered acidification also increases population fitness and promotes cell cycle reentry following heat shock.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6E and 6F showing budding dynamics.

claim: Transcription of heat shock genes can reach as much as a thousand fold during thermal stress.
source: Transcription of heat shock genes surges at the onset of stress, reaching as much as a thousand fold during thermal stress, with more modest induction accompanying nutrient withdrawal and diverse other stresses (Lindquist, 1986; Zid and O'Shea, 2014; Morano et al., 2012; Gidalevitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hsf1 regulates induction of a core group of chaperones in eukaryotes.
source: In eukaryotes, the transcriptional stress response is controlled by multiple factors, with the heat shock transcription factor Hsf1 regulating induction of a core group of chaperones (Solís et al., 2016; Pincus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Basal levels of chaperones repress Hsf1 by direct binding.
source: Basal levels of chaperones repress Hsf1 by direct binding (Shi et al., 1998; Zheng et al., 2016; Krakowiak et al., 2018), and removal of this repression in the absence of stress suffices to activate transcription (Zheng et al., 2016; Krakowiak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Removal of chaperone repression in the absence of stress suffices to activate Hsf1 transcription.
source: Basal levels of chaperones repress Hsf1 by direct binding (Shi et al., 1998; Zheng et al., 2016; Krakowiak et al., 2018), and removal of this repression in the absence of stress suffices to activate transcription (Zheng et al., 2016; Krakowiak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Induced chaperones assist with protein folding and prevent and disperse stress-induced molecular aggregates.
source: Induced chaperones, in turn, assist with protein folding, as well as preventing and dispersing stress-induced molecular aggregates (Vabulas et al., 2010; Richter et al., 2010; Cherkasov et al., 2013; Walters et al., 2015; Kroschwald et al., 2015; Kroschwald et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No specific endogenous eukaryotic protein has been demonstrated to misfold in vivo in response to a sublethal heat shock.
source: Despite the crucial role misfolded proteins play in this model, no specific endogenous eukaryotic protein has been demonstrated to misfold in vivo in response to a sublethal heat shock.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence in the literature.

claim: Newly synthesized polypeptides are thought to serve as Hsf1 inducers during heat stress.
source: Instead, newly synthesized polypeptides (which include nascent chains still being synthesized and complete polypeptides which have yet to reach their native structure) are thought to serve as Hsf1 inducers during heat stress (Baler et al., 1992; Tanabe et al., 1997; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Suppression of newly synthesized polypeptides by translation inhibition suppresses the heat-induced transcription of genes regulated by Hsf1.
source: Suppression of newly synthesized polypeptides by translation inhibition suppresses the heat-induced transcription of genes regulated by Hsf1 (Baler et al., 1992; Beckmann et al., 1992; Albert et al., 2019; Masser et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ongoing translation has been deemed a requirement for Hsf1 activation.
source: Consequently, ongoing translation has been deemed a requirement for Hsf1 activation (Masser et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Diverse environmental changes which stimulate the transcriptional response are accompanied by intracellular acidification.
source: Notably, the same diverse environmental changes which stimulate the transcriptional response are also accompanied by intracellular acidification—a drop in cytosolic pH (Weitzel et al., 1987; Bright and Ellis, 1992; Munder et al., 2016; Kroschwald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stress-induced acidification is broadly conserved in eukaryotes, including mammals, insects, plants, and fungi.
source: Like the transcriptional response, stress-induced acidification is broadly conserved in eukaryotes, including mammals (Bright and Ellis, 1992; Yao and Haddad, 2004; Tombaugh and Sapolsky, 1993; Díaz et al., 2016), insects (Drummond et al., 1986; Zhong et al., 1999), plants (Ishizawa, 2014), and fungi (Weitzel et al., 1987; Kroschwald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies across multiple taxa.

claim: The cytoprotective effects of short-term acidification were identified decades ago.
source: Although acidification has sometimes been viewed as a toxic consequence of stress, particularly in studies of hypoxia and ischemia-associated acidosis (Ishizawa, 2014; Tombaugh and Sapolsky, 1993), the cytoprotective effects of short-term acidification were identified decades ago (Tombaugh and Sapolsky, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Interfering with energy-depletion-induced acidification in budding yeast and fission yeast compromises the fitness of both species.
source: Recent work has shown that interfering with energy-depletion-induced acidification in budding yeast and in fission yeast, which diverged from budding yeast more than half a billion years ago (Hedges et al., 2015), compromises the fitness of both species (Munder et al., 2016; Joyner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Many mature proteins associated with stress-induced condensation show a strong dependence on pH for their self-association.
source: Furthermore, many mature proteins associated with stress-induced condensation show a strong dependence on pH for their self-association, whether by polymerization or phase separation (Petrovska et al., 2014; Kroschwald et al., 2015; Munder et al., 2016; Riback et al., 2017; Franzmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Hsf1 trimerization can be induced by acidification in vitro in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Early work in Drosophila melanogaster produced mixed results: one study indicated that acidification had little impact on the production of heat shock proteins (Drummond et al., 1986), while later work showed that Hsf1 trimerization, a key activation step, could be induced by acidification in vitro (Zhong et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cell cycle reentry after heat shock follows the dissolution of stress granules, which depends on molecular chaperones.
source: What has been demonstrated is that cell cycle reentry after heat shock follows the dissolution of stress granules, which depends on the products of stress-induced transcriptional changes: molecular chaperones (Kroschwald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Yeast cells maintain a resting pH of around 7.5.
source: Yeast thrive in acidic environments, and spend significant cellular resources on the activity of membrane-associated proton pumps which keep the cytoplasm at a resting pH of around 7.5 (Orij et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and confirmed by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The electrochemical gradient in yeast is disrupted during stress, causing cells to acidify.
source: The resulting electrochemical gradient is used to drive transport and other crucial cellular processes, but is disrupted during stress, causing cells to acidify (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 and citations in the text.

claim: Elevated temperature increases membrane permeability in yeast.
source: While the mechanism of proton influx remains poorly understood, elevated temperature increases membrane permeability (Coote et al., 1994) and other stresses have been shown to reduce proton pump activity (Orij et al., 2011; Orij et al., 2012; Dechant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells rapidly and reproducibly acidify from a resting pH of approximately 7.5 to a range of slightly acidic pH values around 6.8 to 7.0 during a 42°C, 10 min heat stress in acidic media.
source: During a 42°C, 10 min heat stress in acidic media (pH 4) we find that cells rapidly and reproducibly acidify from a resting pH of approximately 7.5 to a range of slightly acidic pH values around 6.8 to 7.0 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, in agreement with previous results [Weitzel et al., 1987]).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: When returned to normal growth temperature (30°C), cells restore the resting pH in approximately ten minutes after heat shock.
source: When returned to normal growth temperature (30°C), cells restore the resting pH in approximately ten minutes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ssa4 is a strongly temperature-responsive Hsp70 chaperone.
source: Ssa4 is a strongly temperature-responsive Hsp70 chaperone, and its encoding gene is a specific Hsf1 target (Hottiger et al., 1992; Pincus et al., 2018; Morano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells that could not acidify during stress delayed and reduced the induction of Ssa4.
source: Stressing cells in non-acidic media prevented acidification (Figure 2A). Cells that could not acidify during stress delayed and reduced the induction of Ssa4 (Figure 2D, left hand side).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2D.

claim: Brief glucose withdrawal rapidly and reversibly inhibits translation of most cellular mRNAs in yeast.
source: To test whether acidification still promoted the stress response even under conditions where the concentration of newly synthesized polypeptides would be sharply limited, we first used brief glucose withdrawal, a physiologically relevant condition which is known to rapidly and reversibly inhibit translation of most cellular mRNAs (Ashe et al., 2000 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and confirmed by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells that could acidify during stress responded almost identically to cells stressed while global translation was unperturbed, even in the absence of translation.
source: Strikingly, we found that even in the absence of translation and presumably misfolded newly synthesized polypeptides, cells that could acidify during stress responded almost identically to cells stressed while global translation was unperturbed.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, right hand side.

claim: Cells that were not actively translating and also were unable to acidify during stress almost completely failed to respond.
source: However, cells that were not actively translating and also were unable to acidify during stress almost completely failed to respond (Figure 2D, right hand side).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, right hand side.

claim: When cells were able to acidify, they robustly responded to heat shock regardless of whether they could translate.
source: We found that when cells were able to acidify, they robustly responded to heat shock regardless of whether they could translate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When acidification was prevented, translational repression markedly inhibited the transcriptional response.
source: When acidification was prevented, translational repression markedly inhibited the transcriptional response (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Rapid, robust chaperone expression following heat shock depends either on ongoing translation or on intracellular acidification.
source: From these data we conclude that rapid, robust chaperone expression following heat shock depends either on ongoing translation, as previous studies have found, or on intracellular acidification (Figure 2F), an effect which has not been reported before.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Actively translating cells responded by strongly upregulating heat shock genes independent of the pH during stress.
source: As expected, actively translating cells responded by strongly upregulating heat shock genes identified by previous studies (see Materials and methods for gene annotations) independent of the pH during stress, whereas cycloheximide-treated cells showed reduced induction of heat shock genes when acidification was also blocked (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cycloheximide-treated cells showed reduced induction of heat shock genes when acidification was also blocked.
source: As expected, actively translating cells responded by strongly upregulating heat shock genes identified by previous studies (see Materials and methods for gene annotations) independent of the pH during stress, whereas cycloheximide-treated cells showed reduced induction of heat shock genes when acidification was also blocked (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The pH sensitivity of the Hsf1 regulon is remarkably clear when cells are translationally inhibited.
source: The pH sensitivity of the Hsf1 regulon is remarkably clear when cells are translationally inhibited (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Msn2/4 regulon continues to induce robustly independent of pH and translational status.
source: Because the Msn2/4 regulon continues to induce robustly independent of pH and translational status, a broader effect of pH on transcriptional processes cannot explain Hsf1's sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When translation was inhibited with cycloheximide, Hsf1 became a clear outlier, showing strong acidification-related induction.
source: In translationally active cells, no regulons show much acidification-dependent induction (Figure 3D, left). However, when we inhibited translation with cycloheximide, Hsf1 became a clear outlier, showing strong acidification-related induction (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When translation is arrested during heat shock, Hsf1 is the only transcription factor examined that shows significant sensitivity to acidification.
source: When translation is arrested during heat shock, Hsf1 is the only transcription factor examined that shows significant sensitivity to acidification.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The regulon of transcription factor Ifh1 was pH-sensitive only under conditions where cells were translationally active.
source: Interestingly, the regulon of another transcription factor, Ifh1, was pH-sensitive only under conditions where cells were translationally active (Figure 3E, left hand side).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Repression of the Ifh1 regulon depends on the synthesis of ribosomal proteins.
source: Repression of the Ifh1 regulon depends on the synthesis of ribosomal proteins (Albert et al., 2019); we find that it also depends on intracellular acidification, but unlike Hsf1 this pH sensitivity is not dependent on translational status.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When cellular translation is halted, intracellular acidification specifically promotes induction of genes under control of Hsf1.
source: Most strikingly, when cellular translation is halted—conditions under which classical models predict little or no Hsf1 activation—we find that intracellular acidification specifically promotes induction of genes under control of Hsf1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Nigericin is a K+/H+ antiporter that has been used to equilibrate intracellular and extracellular pH.
source: Nigericin is a K+/H+ antiporter (Freedman, 2012) which has been used in a variety of biological systems to equilibrate intracellular and extracellular pH (Modi et al., 2009; Nakata et al., 2010; Thomas et al., 1979; Christen et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: By placing cells in buffers at different pHs and treating with ionophore, intracellular pH can be accurately manipulated independent of temperature.
source: We verified that by placing cells in buffers at different pHs and treating with ionophore we were able to accurately manipulate intracellular pH, and that this control did not depend on temperature (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ionophore treatment alone did not have long-term fitness consequences.
source: We also verified that ionophore treatment alone did not have long-term fitness consequences by measuring the relative growth rate of treated and untreated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Acidification alone is not sufficient to produce a stress response at physiological pH levels.
source: Manipulating intracellular pH independent of temperature allowed us to determine that acidification alone was not sufficient to produce a stress response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, right hand side), with the exception of the lowest pH examined, pH 5.0, which is substantially below the range of physiologically realized pH values during short-term heat shock (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Figure 1B.

claim: Additional acidification during stress, as low as pH 5, did not increase or decrease the response compared to physiological acidification.
source: Furthermore, we found that additional acidification during stress, as low as pH 5, did not increase or decrease the response compared to physiological acidification.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When cells heat shocked without acidification were allowed to recover in acidic media, they were able to induce Ssa4 where cells recovering in buffered medium were not.
source: Remarkably, when we heat shocked cells and prevented acidification, but allowed them to recover in acidic media, these cells were able to induce Ssa4 where cells recovering in buffered medium were not (Figure 4D, compare to Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4C.

claim: Recovery-media-pH-dependent induction occurred with a pH-dependent delay which was maximal when cells did not experience acidification during stress.
source: This recovery-media-pH-dependent induction occurred with a pH-dependent delay (Figure 4E) which was maximal when cells did not experience acidification during stress.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cells stressed under acidic conditions rapidly restored intracellular pH during recovery.
source: Populations stressed under acidic conditions rapidly restored intracellular pH during recovery (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells stressed at pH values above 7.0 took longer on average to restore intracellular pH to resting levels, and in some cases failed to do so even after two hours.
source: In contrast, cells stressed at pH values above 7.0 took longer on average to restore intracellular pH to resting levels, and in some cases failed to do so even after two hours (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells that had failed to return to the resting pH range also failed to induce Ssa4 on average.
source: We noted that on average, cells that had failed to return to the resting pH range also failed to induce Ssa4 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Virtually all cells that produced high levels of Ssa4 had returned to the resting pH.
source: Examination of the relationship between intracellular pH variation and production of Ssa4 in single cells revealed a clear pattern: virtually all cells that produced high levels of Ssa4 had returned to the resting pH (Figure 5E), and cells which did not return to the resting pH showed low levels of Ssa4 for up to three hours (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The vast majority of cells which had restored the resting pH after 105 min of recovery went on to robustly induce Ssa4.
source: The vast majority of cells which had restored the resting pH after 105 min of recovery went on to robustly induce Ssa4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The lower-expressing subpopulation had a distinctly acid-shifted intracellular pH compared to the high-expressing cells.
source: We found that the lower-expressing subpopulation had a distinctly acid-shifted intracellular pH compared to the high-expressing cells (Figure 5G), confirming our prediction.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Return to the resting pH predicts the dynamics of chaperone production.
source: Return to the resting pH predicts the dynamics of chaperone production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single-cell data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Population growth rate during recovery depended strongly on intracellular pH during heat shock.
source: Population growth rate during recovery depended strongly on intracellular pH during heat shock.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Maximum fitness was achieved by populations with intracellular pH enforced to be close to its observed physiological stress-induced levels (∼6.8).
source: Maximum fitness was achieved by populations with intracellular pH enforced to be close to its observed physiological stress-induced levels (∼6.8) in unmanipulated cells (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The largest fitness defects were observed in populations with pH levels set at pre-stress levels (∼7.5).
source: We observed the largest fitness defects in populations with pH levels set at pre-stress levels (∼7.5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ionophore treatment alone had only a minor, pH-independent effect on cell growth.
source: Ionophore treatment alone had only a minor, pH-independent effect on cell growth (Figure 6B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mimicking physiological intracellular acidification during stress maximizes fitness during recovery.
source: We conclude that mimicking physiological intracellular acidification during stress maximizes fitness during recovery, consistent with acidification playing an adaptive role in the heat shock response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fitness data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Virtually all cells which could be confidently assigned to the budded state showed high chaperone expression.
source: Virtually all cells which could be confidently assigned to the budded state showed high chaperone expression, and nearly all cells showing low chaperone expression were found in the unbudded state.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Low-expression, unbudded cells showed near-uniform reduction in pH.
source: Low-expression, unbudded cells also showed near-uniform reduction in pH (Figure 6D, lower left panel), consistent with the dysregulation of pH observed at the population level.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cells that experienced a more acidic or more basic pH during heat shock showed a delay in the occurrence of the budding peak.
source: However, cells that experienced a more acidic or more basic pH during heat shock showed a delay in the occurrence of the budding peak (Figure 6E, summarized in Figure 6F), in agreement with the difference in growth rates shown in Figure 6B.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6F.

claim: Post-stress resumption of growth is tuned to particular stress-associated cytoplasmic pH values.
source: By measuring growth in multiple ways, we have shown that post-stress resumption of growth is tuned to particular stress-associated cytoplasmic pH values.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fitness and cell cycle data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Fitness positively correlates both with increased chaperone production and with restoration of the pre-stress pH in populations and in individual cells.
source: Moreover, fitness positively correlates both with increased chaperone production and with restoration of the pre-stress pH in populations and in individual cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The canonical transcriptional stress response mediated by Hsf1 depends on cellular acidification.
source: By decoupling changes in intracellular pH from heat shock in budding yeast, we have discovered that the canonical transcriptional stress response mediated by heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) depends on cellular acidification.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: When cells are translationally suppressed, transient acidification becomes a requirement for achieving a robust transcriptional response.
source: When cells are translationally suppressed, such as following glucose withdrawal, transient acidification becomes a requirement for achieving a robust transcriptional response.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Even in translationally active cells, acidification promotes induction of the heat shock response.
source: Even in translationally active cells, acidification promotes induction.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, left hand side.

claim: Restoration of resting pH and chaperone protein expression increase competitive fitness by promoting reentry into the cell cycle and overall population growth rates.
source: Restoration of resting pH and chaperone protein expression increase competitive fitness by promoting reentry into the cell cycle and overall population growth rates, indicating that transient acidification is an adaptive component of the heat shock response.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Transient acidification is an adaptive component of the heat shock response.
source: Restoration of resting pH and chaperone protein expression increase competitive fitness by promoting reentry into the cell cycle and overall population growth rates, indicating that transient acidification is an adaptive component of the heat shock response.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Extracellular protons entering the cell following heat shock are the dominant cause of acidification.
source: Our results strongly indicate that extracellular protons entering the cell following heat shock are the dominant cause of acidification.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2C.

claim: Simply placing translationally inactive cells in medium buffered to the resting cellular pH is sufficient to suppress the heat shock response during an otherwise robust heat shock.
source: Simply placing translationally inactive cells in medium buffered to the resting cellular pH is sufficient to suppress the heat shock response during an otherwise robust heat shock, suggesting that no intracellular store of protons is liberated to cause acidification.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, right hand side.

claim: Proton permeability increases with temperature in S. cerevisiae.
source: Membrane permeability to small molecules increases with temperature in S. cerevisiae (Coote et al., 1994), and proton permeability specifically has been shown to increase with temperature (van de Vossenberg et al., 1999), providing a likely mechanism for temperature-dependent acidification when a plasma-membrane-spanning proton gradient is present.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells must restore their resting pH before producing high levels of molecular chaperones.
source: A surprising yet consistent detail is that cells must restore their resting pH before producing high levels of molecular chaperones.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Intracellular pH controls growth rate in yeast.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that heat shock causes changes in intracellular pH (Weitzel et al., 1985) and that intracellular pH controls growth rate (Orij et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acidification in the absence of heat shock, at least to pH levels which would normally follow heat shock, is insufficient to activate Hsf1.
source: Acidification in the absence of heat shock, at least to pH levels which would normally follow heat shock, is insufficient to activate Hsf1, ruling out direct sensing of pH by Hsf1 or its repressor Hsp70.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Hsf1 can be robustly activated without a drop in pH, so long as cells are translationally active.
source: On the flip side, Hsf1 can be robustly activated without a drop in pH, so long as cells are translationally active, indicating that acidification is not necessary for Hsf1 activation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, left hand side.

claim: Production of Hsp70 binding substrates that titrate Hsp70 away from Hsf1 suffices to induce Hsf1 in the absence of heat shock.
source: Recent key studies have demonstrated that production of Hsp70 binding substrates that titrate Hsp70 away from Hsf1 suffices to induce Hsf1 in the absence of heat shock (Zheng et al., 2016; Krakowiak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous results argue against widespread heat-induced misfolding of mature endogenous proteins in vivo.
source: Previous results argue against widespread heat-induced misfolding of mature endogenous proteins in vivo (Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells show marked repression of the heat shock response at 42°C when translation is attenuated and resting pH is maintained.
source: Here, consistent with those results, cells show marked repression of the heat shock response at 42°C when translation is attenuated and resting pH is maintained, suggesting that misfolding caused by temperature, if it occurs, is insufficient to trigger the Hsf1 response.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, right hand side.

claim: Nearly two hundred mature endogenous proteins in yeast form reversible condensates in response to heat shock.
source: Remarkably, a profusion of such candidates exists. Nearly two hundred mature endogenous proteins in yeast form reversible condensates in response to heat shock which under extreme stress coalesce into stress granules (Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hsp70 colocalizes with stress granules.
source: Hsp70 colocalizes with stress granules (Cherkasov et al., 2013; Walters et al., 2015), and stress-granule dispersal depends on Hsp70 and other chaperones (Cherkasov et al., 2013; Walters et al., 2015; Kroschwald et al., 2015; Kroschwald et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stress-granule dispersal depends on Hsp70 and other chaperones.
source: Hsp70 colocalizes with stress granules (Cherkasov et al., 2013; Walters et al., 2015), and stress-granule dispersal depends on Hsp70 and other chaperones (Cherkasov et al., 2013; Walters et al., 2015; Kroschwald et al., 2015; Kroschwald et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pab1, Pub1, and Ded1 condense by phase separation in vitro when exposed to heat in a pH-dependent manner.
source: Three individual protein components of stress granules, poly(A)-binding protein Pab1, poly(U)-binding protein Pub1, and the DEAD-box RNA helicase Ded1, condense by phase separation in vitro when exposed to heat in a pH-dependent manner (Riback et al., 2017; Kroschwald et al., 2018; Iserman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A 42°C heat shock is insufficient to cause Pab1 condensation at pH 7.5, but sufficient at pH 6.6.
source: For example, a 42°C heat shock is insufficient to cause Pab1 condensation at pH 7.5, but sufficient at pH 6.6 (Riback et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Acidic pH promotes phase separation of Pub1 at non-shock temperatures, but these condensates spontaneously disperse when the resting pH is restored.
source: In the case of Pub1, acidic pH promotes phase separation at non-shock temperatures, but these condensates spontaneously disperse when the resting pH is restored; only heat-triggered Pub1 condensates require dispersal by molecular chaperones (Kroschwald et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Only heat-triggered Pub1 condensates require dispersal by molecular chaperones.
source: In the case of Pub1, acidic pH promotes phase separation at non-shock temperatures, but these condensates spontaneously disperse when the resting pH is restored; only heat-triggered Pub1 condensates require dispersal by molecular chaperones (Kroschwald et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: pH- and temperature-dependent condensing proteins are hypothesized to be the cause of the Hsf1 pH-dependence observed when translation is silenced.
source: Based on these observations, we make three hypotheses to be tested in future work. First, we hypothesize that pH- and temperature-dependent condensing proteins are the cause of the Hsf1 pH-dependence we observe when translation is silenced.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their results and previous literature.

claim: If pH- and temperature-dependent condensing proteins are found, they are predicted to activate Hsf1 by recruiting Hsp70 in the condensed state.
source: Second, we predict that if such proteins are found, they will activate Hsf1 by recruiting Hsp70 in the condensed state.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on their hypothesis.

claim: Many pH- and temperature-dependent condensing proteins are hypothesized to exist, such that it should be possible to activate Hsf1 by triggering condensation of a single protein.
source: Third, we hypothesize that many such proteins exist, such that it should be possible to activate Hsf1 by triggering condensation of a single protein, but that suppression of any single protein's condensation may not suppress Hsf1 activation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Human Hsf1 possesses intrinsic thermal sensing ability regulating its trimerization.
source: Recent work has suggested that human Hsf1 possesses intrinsic thermal sensing ability regulating its trimerization (Hentze et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hsf1 thermosensing has yet to be demonstrated in vivo or for yeast.
source: While this is a tantalizing possibility, Hsf1 thermosensing has yet to be demonstrated in vivo or for yeast, whose Hsf1 is thought to be constitutively trimerized (Morano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Temperature alone is insufficient to activate Hsf1's response when translation is attenuated; a drop in intracellular pH is required.
source: Our results also demonstrate that temperature alone is insufficient to activate Hsf1's response when translation is attenuated; a drop in intracellular pH is required.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phase separation and other phase-transition behaviors provide a compelling solution to the problem of sensing temperature.
source: Phase separation and other phase-transition behaviors provide a compelling solution to the tricky problem of sensing temperature, which typically involves only a few degrees' change: 30°C to 37°C for robust induction of yeast's heat shock response (Gasch et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by a citation.

claim: Phase transitions are highly cooperative, amplifying tiny changes in individual molecules into massive system-level transformations.
source: Phase transitions by definition are highly cooperative, amplifying tiny changes in individual molecules into massive system-level transformations (Yoo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the physical properties of phase transitions, supported by a citation.

claim: Heat-shock-triggered condensation of mature proteins is not suppressed by translational inhibition.
source: Crucially, unlike misfolding of newly synthesized polypeptides, heat-shock-triggered condensation of mature proteins is not suppressed by translational inhibition (Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: More than a dozen proteins form condensates in under two minutes in response to heat shock in vivo in yeast.
source: We have previously identified more than a dozen proteins which form condensates in under two minutes in response to heat shock in vivo (Wallace et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Thermosensitive 'superaggregator' proteins are predicted to condense autonomously, recruit Hsp70 upon condensation, and show condensation behavior that is suppressed at the resting intracellular pH.
source: We predict they will have several characteristics shared by existing less-sensitive proteins: they will condense autonomously (without relying on the temperature-sensitive condensation of other factors), will recruit Hsp70 upon condensation, and will show condensation behavior that is suppressed at the resting intracellular pH.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on their hypothesis.

claim: Artificially induced misfolded proteins can induce the heat shock response.
source: While it is clear that artificially induced misfolded proteins can induce the heat shock response (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011; Trotter et al., 2002), this does not constitute evidence that they serve as inducers under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heat alone is insufficient to trigger the Hsf1 response when translation is attenuated and resting pH is maintained.
source: Here, we have shown that heat alone is insufficient to trigger the Hsf1 response, and that the newly synthesized polypeptides often cited as the primary inducers of Hsf1 are not required for Hsf1 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Newly synthesized polypeptides often cited as the primary inducers of Hsf1 are not required for Hsf1 activation.
source: Here, we have shown that heat alone is insufficient to trigger the Hsf1 response, and that the newly synthesized polypeptides often cited as the primary inducers of Hsf1 are not required for Hsf1 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some dimorphic fungi convert from a mold to a yeast in response to entering a mammalian host and detecting the resulting increase in temperature.
source: For example, some dimorphic fungi live and grow in the environment as a mold, and convert into a yeast (a single-celled, reproducing fungus) in response to entering a mammalian host and detecting the resulting increase in temperature, the critical sensory cue (Klein and Tebbets, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Candida albicans requires a temperature increase to trigger the bud-to-hyphae transition critical for infection.
source: The budding yeast and occasional human pathogen Candida albicans similarly requires a temperature increase to trigger the bud-to-hyphae transition critical for infection (Brown et al., 2010), which also induces chaperones in a classical Hsf1-mediated heat shock response (Nicholls et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S. cerevisiae does not produce fruiting bodies and depends upon animal hosts for dispersal.
source: S. cerevisiae does not produce fruiting bodies and depends upon animal hosts for dispersal (Mortimer and Polsinelli, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A survey of hundreds of migratory passerine birds isolated S. cerevisiae from 14% of cloacal samples.
source: A survey of hundreds of migratory passerine (perching) birds (Francesca et al., 2012) isolated yeast species from their cloacae, implying ingestion as the source; 14% of isolates were Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: S. cerevisiae survived experimental passage through birds when inoculated in feed.
source: S. cerevisiae survived experimental passage through birds when inoculated in feed (Francesca et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Passerine birds have an internal body temperature averaging 41.6°C when active, rising to an average of nearly 44°C during high activity.
source: Passerine birds, the most numerous on earth, have an internal body temperature averaging 41.6°C (range 39°C to 44°C) when active, rising to an average of nearly 44°C (43.1–47.7) during high activity such as running and flight (Prinzinger et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The body temperatures of passerine birds correspond remarkably well to the upper bound of nonlethal temperatures for S. cerevisiae.
source: These temperatures correspond remarkably well to the upper bound of nonlethal temperatures for S. cerevisiae (Salvadó et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A prominent ecological niche for S. cerevisiae is the surface of fruits such as grapes.
source: A prominent ecological niche for S. cerevisiae is the surface of fruits such as grapes (Mortimer and Polsinelli, 1999), which birds eat—indeed, vineyard crop damage by passerine birds is a major challenge for the wine industry (Somers and Morris, 2002; DeHaven and Hothem, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast proliferate to higher numbers on damaged fruit which often results from bird pecking.
source: Yeast proliferate to higher numbers on damaged fruit (Mortimer and Polsinelli, 1999) which often results from bird pecking (Chiurazzi et al., 2010; Somers and Morris, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Known dispersing hosts for the Saccharomyces genus include wasps, bees, ants, and fruit flies.
source: Besides birds, other known dispersing hosts for the Saccharomyces genus include wasps, bees, ants, and fruit flies (Dapporto et al., 2016; Madden et al., 2018; Mortimer and Polsinelli, 1999; Giglioli, 1897; Christiaens et al., 2014), all of which are preyed upon by birds, indicating that yeast may enter an avian carrier by multiple routes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ingestion and dispersal by birds is an ecologically established, physiologically relevant, and likely evolutionarily advantageous heat-shock condition for budding yeast.
source: From these diverse and convergent lines of evidence, we conclude that ingestion and dispersal by birds is an ecologically established, physiologically relevant, and likely evolutionarily advantageous heat-shock condition for budding yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence cited in the text.

claim: Fever triggers the Hsf1-mediated heat shock response in humans.
source: In humans, for example, a key physiological heat shock—fever—triggers the Hsf1-mediated heat shock response (Singh and Hasday, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The apoptotic response of human neutrophils to fever temperatures is sharply dependent on intracellular pH, with acidification promoting survival.
source: Indeed, the apoptotic response of human neutrophils to fever temperatures is sharply dependent on intracellular pH, with acidification promoting survival; local acidification is a hallmark of inflammatory conditions and promotes neutrophil activation (Díaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Local acidification is a hallmark of inflammatory conditions and promotes neutrophil activation.
source: Indeed, the apoptotic response of human neutrophils to fever temperatures is sharply dependent on intracellular pH, with acidification promoting survival; local acidification is a hallmark of inflammatory conditions and promotes neutrophil activation (Díaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The association between cellular stress and cytosolic acidification is adaptive and reflects the dependence of the core Hsf1-mediated transcriptional response on pH.
source: Our results speak to a potentially broad effect: that this association is adaptive, and reflects, at least in part, the dependence of the core Hsf1-mediated transcriptional response on pH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of the study.
